name: Olga Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying software engineering in Vienna, and I live in a one-room flat near the Karlsplatz that my parents rent for me. My week is lectures, programming labs, and a study group I started with five others, where we use an AI tutor to quiz each other before exams. I use AI tools every day, for explaining things, for planning my week, even for choosing what to cook. My dad is a lawyer and my mum is an architect, so they pay for my studies and the flat. I like numbers, so I keep a spreadsheet of my time and money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with five pictures of the next few years. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's a relief for some and a waste of money for others. I'd tell my study group that the tools are still useful, they just aren't magic, so we'd carry on. Online I'd say nothing dramatic, I'd post a graph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel it's the easy mode. My parents' jobs would stay as they are, my degree would give a normal career, and I'd already be good with the tools. I'd still be a bit bored, because a world where nothing changes makes my skills less special.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and improve the study group, maybe invite students from other years. I'd apply for a summer internship at a software firm in Vienna, and I'd keep my spreadsheet going. I'd also try a small freelance job, building a booking page for a friend's cafe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A calm world is a good world to plan in, and I like planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be a bit bored. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd be a bit bored. Why? Because I like being early to things. If AI turns out to be hype, being early is worth less, and I'd be one of many who are okay at coding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stand out then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make you stand out then? Doing real projects for real people, like the cafe booking page. A student with three live projects is more interesting than a student with great marks.

say: I'd say it's **useful**, not magic, so we carry on.
Online I'd post a **graph**, not a drama.
think: It's **easy mode**: my parents' jobs and my degree stay normal.
A world where nothing changes makes my **skills less special**.
do: Improve my **study group** and invite students from other years.
Apply for a summer **internship** at a Vienna software firm.
Build a booking page for a friend's **cafe** as freelance work.
feel: **Calm**; a calm world is a good world to plan in.
S0.quote: A student with three live projects is more interesting than a student with great marks.
fieldNote: Olga is **calm** but bored; her edge is being early, and a plateau erodes it.
Her answer to being average is real projects for real people.
She tracks everything in spreadsheets, a sign of planning as her coping tool.

steps.text: Apply for a summer internship at a software firm in Vienna
Build a booking page for a friend's cafe
Invite students from other years to the study group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and we should get ready, and I'd mean it. In the study group I'd say let's put more time into the stuff machines can't do yet, like talking to clients. Online I'd share what's working, because I like to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd worry less about me and more about my parents. Law and architecture are mostly thinking tasks: drafting, checking, drawing plans. My dad says clients are already asking why a contract takes three weeks when a tool does it in an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools even more, and learn how to check them, so I'm the person who can catch mistakes. I'd also start a side project that earns something, so I'm not relying on a single path. And I'd have an honest talk with my parents about their plans, which I'd rather avoid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a mix of excitement about the tools and a heavy feeling about my parents' jobs. I'd keep that second part to myself most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your parents think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What do your parents think? My mum says buildings still need people to look at the ground. My dad says law will become advice, not drafting. They both say it calmly, but my dad has started reading about cybersecurity law, which is not a coincidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to them? That I could be the one who helps them learn the tools, since I know them. It would reverse the roles, which is funny, but they'd like it.

say: I'd say it's **happening** and we should spend more time on what machines can't do, like talking to clients.
think: I worry less about me and more about my **parents'** work.
Law and architecture are mostly **thinking tasks**: drafting, checking, drawing.
do: Use the tools more and learn to **check** them, to catch mistakes.
Start a **side project** that earns something.
Have an honest talk with my **parents** about their plans.
feel: **Uneasy**: excited about the tools, heavy about my parents' jobs.
S1.quote: My dad says law will become advice, not drafting.
fieldNote: Her adaptive streak gives her **ideas**; her worry is about the household's income.
She'd reverse roles by teaching her parents the tools.
Her dad's reading about cybersecurity law shows how close the pressure is.

steps.text: Learn to check AI-written code and contracts for mistakes
Start a paid side project building booking pages
Talk to my parents about their plans and savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules and a safety net now, because there is no time. In the study group I'd say we should be practical: calculate what we can afford and what we can't. And I'd say it to my parents with numbers on a page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel it's a very close call. Both my parents work in thinking jobs, and both could be hit within two years. I'd graduate into a world where entry jobs mostly don't exist, and my parents' income, which pays for me, would be uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with my parents with a spreadsheet and work out how long the family can hold on. I'd cut my own costs, like moving to a shared flat. I'd put all my effort into a business of my own, because working for someone is the riskiest bet. And I'd stay in the degree for the contacts and a diploma.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but my head stays clear. I think better with numbers on a page, and I'd keep making lists to avoid the sinking feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you move out of the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why would you move out of the flat? Because it costs 900 euros a month and my parents might not have a stable income. A shared flat saves 400 euros a month, which is a lot if things go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad? That I'll help if I can, and it's okay to ask. He's proud, and I think I'd have to say it twice.

say: I'd say we need **rules** and a **safety net** now, because there's no time.
I'd tell my parents, with **numbers on a page**.
think: Both parents work in **thinking jobs** and both could be hit within two years.
Entry jobs would mostly not exist, and the **family income** would be uncertain.
do: Sit down with my parents and a **spreadsheet** to work out how long we can hold.
Move into a **shared flat** to save 400 euros a month.
Put my effort into a **business of my own**.
feel: **Anxious**, with a clear head; lists keep the sinking feeling away.
S2.quote: A shared flat saves 400 euros a month, which is a lot if things go wrong.
fieldNote: Her reaction is **numbers first**: a spreadsheet, a smaller flat, a business of her own.
She sees both her parents' jobs as exposed, so the cushion could vanish.
Pride in her dad means she has to offer help twice.

steps.text: Work out with my parents how long the family can hold on
Move from my one-room flat into a shared flat
Launch a small booking-page business with three cafes
Cut my monthly spending by a quarter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if we start immediately. I'd say it to my parents: we should plan for 2031 now. And to my friends: learn the tools and the people skills at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel it gives me a decent chance, but not for my parents. They'd still be mid-career in 2031. I'd graduate in 2029, with maybe a year or two of work before the big date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and go for jobs that involve clients, not just code. I'd set up an investment account with part of my freelance earnings. And I'd help my parents think about what they'd do, like my dad moving to advice work and my mum to site supervision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. I'd like to say I'm sure, but I'm not. I'd feel a bit like I'm running a project with a hard deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said invest. Why that, not just save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said invest. Why that, not just save? Because cash loses value, and my parents' investments are mostly property. I'd want something that moves differently, though I'm not an expert yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who isn't prepared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who isn't prepared? To start with one thing: pick one tool, use it every day for a month. Small steps, and not wait for a perfect plan.

say: I'd say five years is enough if we start **immediately**.
I'd tell friends to learn the tools and the **people skills** together.
think: It gives me a **decent chance**, but my parents would still be mid-career in 2031.
I'd graduate in 2029 and have **a year or two** of work before the date.
do: Go for jobs that involve **clients**, not just code.
Put part of my freelance earnings into an **investment account**.
Help my parents plan: Dad to **advice work**, Mum to site supervision.
feel: **Uneasy**, like running a project with a hard deadline.
S3.quote: Pick one tool, use it every day for a month.
fieldNote: She treats five years like a **project** with a deadline and a budget.
Her investing idea comes from her parents' property-heavy portfolio.
Pushes small steps instead of perfect plans.

steps.text: Aim for client-facing software jobs when applying in final year
Put part of my freelance earnings into an index fund
Sketch a career change plan with each of my parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and I'd be surprised if people spend it well. I'd tell my study group to build skills and savings quietly, because it's less stressful than panic. Online I'd post a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good. I'd have ten years of career, my parents would be near the end of theirs, and I'd have time to build a business. It almost feels like an advantage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a few years at a firm, and start a company around 25. I'd keep using the tools to learn fast. I'd also invest regularly, and I'd help my parents think through retirement so we don't scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of excitement. Ten years is the amount of time I'd choose if someone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk to that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What's the risk to that plan? That I get complacent. If I'm always the early one, I might forget to look at what the world actually needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you avoid complacency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How would you avoid complacency? Ask customers, not classmates. And rebuild my spreadsheet every year, because it makes me look at the numbers again.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** of time, if people spend it well.
I'd tell my study group to build skills and **savings** quietly.
think: I'd have ten years of career, and my parents would be near the **end of theirs**.
do: Finish the degree and work for a **firm** for a few years.
Invest **regularly** and help my parents plan retirement.
feel: **Calm**, with some excitement; ten years is the amount I'd choose.
fieldNote: With a decade, Olga sees an **advantage**; her only fear is complacency.
She links retirement planning for her parents with her own plans.
Customers over classmates: she wants real feedback.

steps.text: Work at a software firm for three years after graduating
Start a small company around age 25
Invest a fixed amount every month in an index fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because both my parents are in thinking jobs and I'd be mid-degree. The longer ones let me plan, and I like plans. What would help is a safety net for families, retraining that's paid for, and for someone to be honest about which jobs go first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people think students like me are all excited about AI. I'm excited about the tools, but I'm worried about my parents, and those two feelings are both true.

headlineQuote: I'm excited about the tools, but I'm worried about my parents, and those two feelings are both true.
portrait: Olga is an 18-year-old **software engineering** student in Vienna who uses AI tools every day and runs a study group.
Her parents, a lawyer and an architect, pay for her studies, so her **cushion is strong**.
She is pragmatic and adaptive: she plans with **spreadsheets** and tests ideas with real projects.
Her worry is that both parents work in **thinking jobs**, which turns fast AGI into real alarm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, since both her parents' jobs could be hit within two years.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **family safety net**, paid retraining and honest word on which jobs go first.
